variants.name: JPA @Version token
variants.implementation_notes: The provider does the work: annotate exactly one @Version field or property (int, Integer, short, long, Long or java.sql.Timestamp) on the entity; it serves as the optimistic lock value, is read with the row, and is appended to the WHERE clause of every UPDATE/DELETE the provider emits, so flush/merge raises OptimisticLockException when the stored version has moved. No lock API is called - the check is implicit in every entity write, which is why Java usually needs no additional structure. Since Jakarta EE 9 the annotation lives in jakarta.persistence.
pitfalls: A version property must be mapped once per class and only on the root entity of an inheritance hierarchy; more than one @Version is non-portable by the specification.
Bulk JPQL/CriteriaUpdate and native queries bypass the version check - the classic hole in an otherwise fully guarded model.
OptimisticLockException marks the transaction for rollback: the persistence context is unusable afterwards and any retry must start in a fresh transaction.

variants.name: Hibernate field-comparison locking
variants.implementation_notes: Hibernate can compare state instead of a token: the @OptimisticLocking annotation selects how lock checking works - VERSION (default), DIRTY (restrict the check to the fields actually changed) or ALL (compare all fields) - and a failure is reported as an optimistic lock exception because the database reports zero rows updated. Attributes can be excluded with @OptimisticLock(excluded = true). It fits legacy schemas that cannot take a version column; VERSION remains the cheapest and most robust choice.
pitfalls: DIRTY/ALL widen the WHERE clause with every mutable column: NULL semantics, floating-point and LOB comparisons make the check brittle and slow.
Excluding a field from optimistic locking means a stale value for it can be written with no signal - exclusions are a deliberate loss of safety.
The check runs at flush time, so a failure surfaces as a rollback-mandated exception on the transaction, not on the setter that caused it.
